territory: Cross-cutting chaos-lite lens: outage and degradation behavior argued end-to-end from code — DB slow/down (error boundaries, mid-submit, mid-scroll), R2 500/429 on every upload/delete path, Resend down or budget exhausted (queue, signup, reset, verify), session expiry mid-form (letter composer, catchup answer, settings), Turnstile unreachable (client and server paths), Upstash down, crons double-fired/missed, Razorpay/Resend webhooks duplicated/delayed, Sentry quota, PostHog proxy.

findings.title: Mail queue burns all 4 retry attempts within a single drain pass — any transient Resend failure permanently kills queued mail, including password resets
findings.expected: MAX_ATTEMPTS=4 spreads retries over time so a transient provider failure (a 30-second Resend 500 streak, or Resend's own ~2-req/s rate limit answering 429 under concurrent drains) is ridden out, and mail sends when the provider recovers.
findings.actual: The drain loop re-picks the SAME row immediately after a failed attempt, so all 4 attempts are spent within seconds of one drain pass; the row flips to terminal status 'failed' and is never retried when Resend recovers. There is no backoff column, no delay, and no next-attempt-at concept anywhere.
findings.evidence: drainMailQueue's loop (email-queue.ts:461-483) runs `for (let i = 0; i < BATCH; i++)` (BATCH=8) and each iteration does `findFirst({ where: { status: "queued", ..., attempts: { lt: MAX_ATTEMPTS } }, orderBy: [{ priority: "asc" }, { createdAt: "asc" }] })`. claimAndSend on failure sets `status: afterFailure` where `afterFailure = spent >= MAX_ATTEMPTS ? "failed" : "queued"` (lines 173-174, 222-226) — a requeued row keeps its createdAt, so the next iteration's findFirst returns the identical row (same priority, still oldest). Four consecutive iterations exhaust attempts 1→4 and the fourth writes terminal `status: "failed"`. Nothing ever retries a 'failed' row: the drain filter is `status: "queued"`. Amplifiers: (a) every authenticated page view schedules a drain (`after(drainMailQueue)` in (main)/layout.tsx:63-69) and every enqueue schedules another (scheduleDrain, email-queue.ts:350), so on launch day many drains run concurrently, each claiming different rows and collectively exceeding Resend's ~2 req/s → 429s that count as failed attempts; (b) dailyBudget (lines 452-475) is read non-atomically per drain, so N concurrent drains can each see remaining=1 and collectively overshoot the 5-message headroom (DAILY_CAP=95 vs 100), producing hard Resend rejections that also burn attempts. Member outcome: a password-reset requester (logged out, no banner to help them) waits at 'check your inbox' forever — the verify banner at least maps 'failed' to a resend offer, but resets have no equivalent surface.
findings.fixDirection: Add a `nextAttemptAt DateTime` (or reuse claimedAt) to OutboundEmail; on a failed send set it to now + backoff (e.g. 2^attempts minutes) and add `nextAttemptAt: { lte: now }` to the drain's findFirst so a failed row cannot be re-picked in the same pass. Distinguish transient provider failures (429/5xx/network) from permanent ones (invalid address) and only count permanent ones against MAX_ATTEMPTS, or raise MAX_ATTEMPTS with real backoff. Add a small jittered serialization (or a single-drainer advisory claim row) so concurrent page-view drains do not collectively exceed Resend's request rate; alternatively add an inter-send sleep inside the BATCH loop.
findings.gateOrTest: New unit test against email-queue drain logic (extract the pick/claim decision into a pure -rule file per repo convention): given a queued row that fails transiently, assert the same pass does not attempt it twice and that a 'failed' verdict requires attempts separated by backoff. Pin with a regression test in src/lib/security-regressions.test.mjs style.
findings.reproPlan: code-argument-only (simulating a Resend outage would require sending real mail or mutating the shared production queue).

findings.title: Client mutation/fetch handlers do not catch server-action rejections — a transient network/DB failure strands the UI: feed skeleton forever, bricked Post button, stuck save status
findings.expected: When a server action's POST fails in transit (mobile network blip — the membership is in India on mobile data — or DB down making the action throw server-side), the member sees an error with a retry, and pending state resets.
findings.actual: A rejected server-action promise is unhandled at these call sites, so the pending flag set before the await is never cleared and no message appears: the feed shows its loading skeleton indefinitely; the composer's Post button stays disabled with no toast; the catchup answer's save indicator sticks on 'saving'. Recovery requires a full page reload.
findings.evidence: post-feed.tsx initial load: `fetchPosts(null).then((data) => { ... setLoading(false); ... })` (lines 118-138) has NO .catch — `loading` starts true (line 57), so a rejection leaves the skeleton forever; React error boundaries do not catch async rejections. handleLoadMore (lines 152-159): `setLoadingMore(true); const data = await fetchPosts(cursor); ... setLoadingMore(false);` with no try/finally — a rejection strands `loadingMore=true` and the button renders disabled 'Loading...' permanently (lines 312-315). create-post-form handleSubmit (lines 497-596): `setSubmitting(true)` then bare `await createPost(formData)` / `await editPost(...)` / `await publishDraft(...)` with no try/catch/finally — a rejection never reaches `setSubmitting(false)` (line 595) and the submit button (`disabled={!content.trim() || submitting || savingDraft}`, line 1059/1087) is dead with zero feedback; contrast login-client.tsx handleSubmit which correctly wraps in try/catch/finally. answer-experience.tsx persist (lines 93-102): handles a RETURNED `{error}` but `await submitEntry(...)` rejection skips both the toast and `setSaveStatus("idle")`, stranding 'saving'. These actions all throw server-side on any Prisma failure (e.g. createPost's `prisma.post.create` at feed/actions.ts:153 has no try/catch), which the Next action transport surfaces as a client-side rejection.
findings.failure_scenario: A member on flaky 4G opens /feed; the loadPosts POST times out → skeleton shimmers forever with no error and no retry. Or: mid-post-submit the DB blips → the Post button greys out permanently, the member's text is still in the editor but nothing tells them what happened.
findings.fixDirection: Establish one pattern and apply it at every server-action await in client components: wrap in try/catch/finally, reset pending state in finally, and toast a generic 'That didn't go through — check your connection and try again' on rejection. For post-feed's initial load add .catch that sets an error state with a visible retry button instead of the skeleton. Grep target: every `await <action>(` inside src/components and src/app/**/*.tsx client files; the four sites above are confirmed, others likely follow the same shape.
findings.gateOrTest: Playwright spec: intercept/abort the action POST route and assert the feed shows an error+retry (geometry/text assertion per repo convention) rather than a skeleton after N seconds; same for the composer button re-enabling.
findings.reproPlan: Safe live proof: chrome-devtools MCP → load /feed signed in, use emulate/network offline just before scroll-triggered load-more (read-only), observe stuck 'Loading...' button and console unhandled rejection.

findings.title: Email case normalization is inconsistent across signup, login and reset — a member whose stored email contains an uppercase letter can never reset their password, silently
findings.expected: One address is one account regardless of typed case: signup, login and password reset all resolve 'John@Gmail.com' and 'john@gmail.com' to the same row.
findings.actual: Signup stores the email exactly as typed (no lowercasing anywhere in the pipeline); login looks the row up case-sensitively with the exact string typed; the forgot-password flow lowercases before lookup. So a mixed-case account (a) requires the identical casing to sign in, (b) NEVER matches in requestPasswordReset — which by anti-enumeration design returns the same { ok: true } and shows 'check your inbox', so no mail ever comes and no error is ever shown, and (c) the same mailbox can register twice under different casings (User.email unique is a plain case-sensitive Postgres unique).
findings.evidence: registerUser: `signupSchema` validates with `z.email(...)` only (validators.ts:18 — no .toLowerCase()/transform), and the row is created with `email: parsed.data.email` (actions.ts:149) after a case-sensitive `findUnique({ where: { email: parsed.data.email } })` (actions.ts:103). authorize(): `await prisma.user.findUnique({ where: { email } })` (auth.ts:102) with the raw credential string — only the rate-limit key is lowercased (`const acctKey = email.trim().toLowerCase()`, auth.ts:62). requestPasswordReset: `const raw = ((formData.get("email") as string) ?? "").trim().toLowerCase(); ... prisma.user.findUnique({ where: { email: raw } })` (email-actions.ts:160-167) and on miss silently `return { ok: true }` (line 172) — deliberate anti-oracle, which is exactly what makes this failure invisible. schema.prisma:13: `email String @unique` (no citext, no lower() expression index found in prisma/migrations-manual/). The human-pass is NOT affected (signHumanPass lowercases internally, human-pass-rule.ts:16), which shows the intended convention the other three paths missed.
findings.failure_scenario: An older alumnus types 'Ravi.Menon@gmail.com' on desktop at signup. Months later they forget their password, type 'ravi.menon@gmail.com' into /forgot-password, see 'check your inbox', and no mail ever arrives — repeatedly, forever. Support cannot see why without inspecting the row.
findings.fixDirection: Normalize (trim + toLowerCase) the email at all three write/lookup points: in signupSchema via z.transform, in authorize() before findUnique, and keep reset as-is. Then run a one-time read of `SELECT id, email FROM "User" WHERE email <> lower(email)` and migrate those rows to lowercase (checking for collisions first). Optionally add a lower(email) unique expression index in migrations-manual to enforce it at the DB.
findings.gateOrTest: Unit test in the .test.mjs suite on the normalization helper; a security-regressions-style pin asserting authorize and requestPasswordReset both lowercase before lookup.
findings.reproPlan: Read-only live proof of standing impact: run `SELECT count(*) FROM "User" WHERE email <> lower(email)` against the DB (read-only) — any nonzero count is a member already in the broken state.

findings.title: Letter autosave fails silently: on any error the desk keeps saying 'Saving...', nothing is surfaced, and a fresh (never-saved) letter has zero draft protection
findings.expected: The immersive letter desk (20,000-char compositions) either saves reliably or tells the writer loudly that saving has stopped; the owner's chaos question 'is the half-written letter lost?' should be answerable with 'no'.
findings.actual: Two gaps. (1) Resumed-draft autosave: `const result = await editPost(postId, fd); if (!result.error) onAutosaveState?.("saved")` — when result.error is set (e.g. 'Not authenticated' after the session was revoked, which the app's own credentialVersion mechanism does instantly on a password reset or deletion request from another device) NOTHING happens: no toast, no state change, the desk chrome stays on 'Saving...' (letter-desk.tsx:55) while every subsequent autosave also fails; a transport rejection additionally goes unhandled (no try/catch). The writer continues for an hour believing the letter is persisting; navigating away loses everything since the last good save. (2) A FRESH letter at /letters/new has no row, so no autosave, no localStorage fallback, and no beforeunload guard (grep for beforeunload across components/posts and components/letters returns nothing) — a crash, an accidental Back, or a session end discards the entire composition.
findings.evidence: create-post-form.tsx:218-227: `autosaveTimer.current = setTimeout(async () => { ... onAutosaveState?.("saving"); ... const result = await editPost(postId, fd); if (!result.error) onAutosaveState?.("saved"); }, 2500);` — the error branch is empty and the await is uncaught. letter-desk.tsx:54-56 renders `{saveState === "saving" ? "Saving..." : ...}` from exactly that callback. The session-revocation interaction is real and by design: auth.ts session callback returns invalid (→ auth() null → editPost returns { error: "Not authenticated" }) the moment credentialVersion changes (auth.ts:277-281), e.g. resetPassword's `credentialVersion: { increment: 1 }` (email-actions.ts:280).
findings.failure_scenario: A member's session is ended (password reset on their phone; or simply signs out in another tab) while a letter draft sits open on the laptop. Every autosave from then on returns 'Not authenticated'; the desk says 'Saving...' indefinitely; an hour of writing is gone when the tab closes.
findings.fixDirection: In the autosave callback: wrap in try/catch; on result.error or rejection set a third autosave state ('failed') that letter-desk renders loudly ('Not saving — check your connection / sign in again'), and toast once on first failure. Mirror the typed content into localStorage keyed by postId (and a 'new-letter' key for fresh compositions) as a crash net; offer restore on next mount. Consider a beforeunload prompt while unsaved changes exist.
findings.gateOrTest: Playwright: open a draft, block the action route, type, assert the failed-save state becomes visible within one autosave interval (expect.poll on the status text).
findings.reproPlan: Safe live proof on a test/admin account: open /letters/[id]/edit for a scratch draft, use chrome-devtools request blocking on the page's action endpoint, type, watch 'Saving...' persist with no error.

findings.title: Turnstile script blocked client-side means nobody can sign in from that browser — with a misleading 'refresh and try once more' message and a 12s stall per attempt
findings.expected: The widget's own header comment promises 'a broken third party never bricks sign-in': if the script cannot load, the form submits without a token and the server 'lets it pass if Turnstile itself is what broke'.
findings.actual: That promise only holds for a SERVER-side Cloudflare failure. When the CLIENT cannot load the script (corporate proxy, DNS filter, aggressive privacy extension blocking challenges.cloudflare.com), getToken() settles null, the form submits with no token, and the server hard-refuses: verifyTurnstile has `if (!token) return false` (turnstile.ts:86, and the file header states 'A request with NO token is refused in both environments alike'). The member gets BOT_CHECK_FAILED — 'We couldn't confirm you're human. Refresh the page and try once more.' — which is false advice: refreshing changes nothing, and the member is permanently locked out from that network/browser with no hint that their blocker is the cause. When the script load HANGS rather than erroring, each attempt first waits out the 12s getToken timeout (turnstile-widget.tsx:139-143).
findings.evidence: turnstile-widget.tsx comment lines 18-21: 'If the script cannot load or the challenge errors, getToken() settles to null and the form submits without a token: the server is the judge anyway, and its own posture ... matches — a broken third party never bricks sign-in.' vs turnstile.ts:86 `if (!token) return false;` and authorize() (auth.ts:83-94): `humanPassValid(...) || devBypassAllowed(...) || (await verifyTurnstile(credentials?.turnstileToken ...)); if (!human) { throw new BotCheckFailed(); }` — a no-token login from a script-blocked browser has none of the three. bot-check-message.ts:10-11 is the sentence shown.
findings.failure_scenario: An alumnus behind a corporate proxy that blocks challenges.cloudflare.com types correct credentials, waits 12 seconds, reads 'refresh and try once more', loops forever, concludes their account is broken.
findings.fixDirection: Owner decision needed on posture: either (a) accept the lockout but fix the copy for the no-token case — client knows the script failed (dead ref) and can show 'Your network or an extension is blocking our human-check (challenges.cloudflare.com). Allow it and retry' before submitting; or (b) treat a MISSING token differently from a failed verification server-side (e.g. allow missing-token logins under a stricter per-IP/account rate limit). At minimum align the widget comment with the real behavior and skip the 12s wait once loadScript has rejected.
findings.gateOrTest: e2e spec with request-blocking on the Turnstile script asserting the pre-submit guidance appears (once fixed); unit test pinning verifyTurnstile(null) behavior stays deliberate.
findings.reproPlan: Safe live proof: chrome-devtools MCP on /login with network request blocking for challenges.cloudflare.com/*, attempt sign-in with the dev account, observe the 12s stall then BOT_CHECK_FAILED.

findings.title: Account purge counts failed R2 deletes as deleted: an R2 outage (or function timeout) during purge silently orphans a deleted member's images at public URLs forever, with a false audit record
findings.expected: GDPR-motivated erasure (the file's own stated purpose) either deletes the R2 bytes or records that it could not, so the objects can be found and removed later.
findings.actual: The DB rows are deleted first (correct, argued in the file), then `for (const url of urls) { await delImage(url); deleted += 1; }` — delImage → delImageByKey swallows every failure in a bare `catch { /* best-effort cleanup */ }` with not even a console line (storage.ts:225-227), and `deleted` increments unconditionally. If R2 returns 500/429 during the nightly purge, every object survives at its public pub-*.r2.dev URL, the rows that pointed at them are already cascaded away ('afterwards nothing can enumerate the objects' — the file's own words), and the audit entry writes 'N stored image(s) removed' (retention.ts:132) when zero were. A function timeout mid-loop (the sweep runs 7 deleteManys plus per-account purges with sequential per-object round trips, no maxDuration set anywhere) truncates the loop the same way.
findings.evidence: account-purge.ts:108-113: `let deleted = 0; for (const url of urls) { await delImage(url); deleted += 1; } return { ok: true, imagesDeleted: deleted };` — the comment above it claims 'the audit entry the CALLER writes records how many objects were actually removed', which the code does not do. storage.ts:218-228: `export async function delImageByKey(key) { try { ... DeleteObjectCommand ... } catch { // best-effort cleanup } }` — no logging.
findings.failure_scenario: R2 has a bad ten minutes at 21:00 UTC on a night the sweep purges a member with 40 Collection photos. All 40 remain publicly fetchable forever; the audit log says '40 stored image(s) removed'; nobody can ever find them again.
findings.fixDirection: Make delImageByKey return success/failure (and log failures); in purgeUserAccount count only true deletions and, before the row delete, persist the collected URL list to a small PurgeQueue table (or the AuditLog detail) so a later retry can finish the job; have the retention sweep retry outstanding object deletions. Report imagesFailed alongside imagesDeleted in the audit detail.
findings.gateOrTest: Unit test on a refactored delImage that surfaces failure; a sweep-level test asserting a failed delete leaves a retryable record.
findings.reproPlan: code-argument-only (cannot safely exercise deletes against the production bucket).

findings.title: Orphaned R2 objects accumulate with no cleanup: abandoned staging uploads, partial finalize failures, validation-refused contributions, and DB-write-after-upload failures all leak publicly fetchable bytes
findings.expected: Objects written to R2 either end up referenced by a DB row or get cleaned up; at 2,000 users the bucket does not grow unbounded with unreachable (but publicly fetchable) member photos.
findings.actual: Several confirmed leak paths, and no lifecycle rule, reconciliation job, or cleanup sweep exists anywhere in the repo (no reference to staging cleanup in retention.ts, docs/spec/media.md, or any cron): (1) presigned PUT completes but the member closes the tab before finalize/contribute → object sits under staging/ or collection/ forever; (2) finalize's multi-file loop: for keys [A,B], A is processed and its display WebP written to uploads/ (route line 116), then B fails → the route returns 422 with no urls, A's WebP is orphaned, and the finally block deleted BOTH staged originals — so retry means full re-upload and the orphan stays; (3) contributePhotoDirect: the photoSchema validation failure at line 297 `return { error: parsed.error... }` does NOT delete the staged original (the quota branch at 282-287 does — the asymmetry is the bug); (4) any path where putImage succeeds and the subsequent prisma write fails (contributePhotoDirect's photo.create at line 377, updateAvatar's user.update at 246) orphans the fresh objects; (5) composer uploads whose post is never created.
findings.evidence: finalize/route.ts:83-125: per-key loop `urls.push(url)` then on a later key's failure `return NextResponse.json({ error ... }, { status: 422 })` inside the loop with `finally { await delImageByKey(key); }` — already-pushed urls are never cleaned and never returned. collection/actions.ts:289-297: `const parsed = photoSchema.safeParse({...}); if (!parsed.success) return { error: parsed.error.issues[0].message };` with no delImageByKey(input.key), unlike the quota branch directly above (lines 283-287). No cleanup exists: grep for 'staging' across retention.ts and the crons returns nothing.
findings.failure_scenario: Over months at 2k users, thousands of unreferenced objects accumulate — storage cost, and a privacy wrinkle: an abandoned staged original (full-resolution, EXIF/GPS intact — the re-encode that strips EXIF only happens on finalize) remains fetchable at a guessable-only-by-key public URL indefinitely.
findings.fixDirection: Two-pronged: (a) add an R2 lifecycle rule (dashboard, owner action) expiring staging/ objects after 24h — this catches most leaks structurally; (b) fix the code asymmetries: delete the staged key on ANY early return in contributePhotoDirect, and in finalize clean up already-processed WebPs when a later key fails (or return partial urls). Optionally add a weekly reconciliation listing bucket keys not referenced by any row (Photo, User.photoUrl, Post.images, CatchupEntry.images).
findings.gateOrTest: Unit test on the finalize loop's failure path asserting compensating deletes; an operational check in the admin worklist showing bucket-vs-rows drift if the reconciliation is built.
findings.reproPlan: Read-only live proof: list the bucket's staging/ prefix (read-only S3 ListObjects with existing creds) and check for objects older than a day.

findings.title: DB outage during login is reported as 'Invalid email or password', sending members into a doomed reset loop
findings.expected: An infrastructure failure at sign-in reads as 'something is wrong on our side, try again shortly' — the login client's own comment says telling someone their password is wrong when it isn't 'sends them into a doomed reset loop'.
findings.actual: authorize() throws raw Prisma errors (e.g. `prisma.user.findUnique` at auth.ts:102, pool timeout, connection refused) — these are not CredentialsSignin subclasses, so NextAuth surfaces a generic error result with no code; the client maps every non-'rate-limited'/non-'bot-check' error to the literal string 'Invalid email or password.' The member re-types the password, fails again, then requests a reset — which during the same DB outage also cannot work (and whose anti-oracle design shows success regardless).
findings.evidence: login-client.tsx:391-398: `const code = (result as { code?: string | null }).code; setError(code === "rate-limited" ? RATE_LIMITED : code === "bot-check" ? BOT_CHECK_FAILED : "Invalid email or password.");` — the fallback branch is reached for ANY error without those two codes, including NextAuth's wrapping of a thrown database error (CallbackRouteError/Configuration), not just a genuine credential refusal. auth.ts defines only the two CredentialsSignin subclasses (lines 21-26); every other throw in authorize is unclassified.
findings.failure_scenario: Supabase has a 2-minute blip at peak evening IST. Every member who tries to sign in is told their password is wrong; several start password resets; a few conclude their account was deleted.
findings.fixDirection: In login-client, distinguish the credential-refusal code path from the unknown-error path: NextAuth returns the error type in result.error — treat anything that is not the CredentialsSignin flavor (or: anything where code is absent AND error is not 'CredentialsSignin') as 'We're having trouble on our end. Please try again in a moment.' Optionally add a third CredentialsSignin subclass server-side wrapping infrastructure failures explicitly.
findings.gateOrTest: Unit-level test of the client mapping function (extract it); e2e with the auth route intercepted to return a 500 asserting the neutral message.
findings.reproPlan: Safe live proof: chrome-devtools on /login, block or 500 the /api/auth/callback/credentials request via request interception, submit dev credentials, read the rendered error text.

findings.title: Feed time filters ('Today', 'This week/month/year') use UTC day boundaries — wrong by 5.5 hours for the IST membership
findings.expected: A member in India filtering the feed to 'Today' sees posts since their midnight (IST).
findings.actual: getTimeFilterDate runs on the server (Vercel, TZ=UTC): `new Date(now.getFullYear(), now.getMonth(), now.getDate())` is UTC midnight = 05:30 IST. 'Today' at 9am IST silently excludes everything posted between 00:00 and 05:30 IST; 'This week' starts Sunday-UTC (05:30 IST Sunday); 'This month'/'This year' shift the same way, and for the first 5.5 hours of the 1st the 'This month' filter still shows last month's boundary. The same server-local-midnight pattern (`setHours(0,0,0,0)`) appears in the admin dashboard month windows (admin/page.tsx:65, admin/support/page.tsx:40) — admin-only, but the same class.
findings.evidence: feed/actions.ts:747-759: `case "today": return new Date(now.getFullYear(), now.getMonth(), now.getDate());` etc., invoked server-side from loadPosts (line 781) — server components/actions run in UTC on Vercel; members are IST (brief). This is precisely the tracked raw-SQL-timestamp-trap's 'deeper IST instances ARE in scope' class.
findings.failure_scenario: A member posts at 1:00am IST; at 8am IST another member filters 'Today' and the post is missing, though the feed unfiltered shows it timestamped 'today'.
findings.fixDirection: Compute the boundary in IST: either pass the client's UTC offset with the filter request (the composer already runs client-side), or hard-code Asia/Kolkata (the community is single-timezone by charter) via e.g. a small helper that shifts now by +5:30 before truncating to the day and shifts back. Apply the same helper to the admin month windows.
findings.gateOrTest: Unit test on an extracted istDayStart helper across the 00:00-05:30 IST window (repo already has the .test.mjs pattern).
findings.reproPlan: code-argument-only (a live proof needs a post created inside the 00:00-05:30 IST window).

findings.title: Concurrent same-batch signups can create duplicate 'Batch of {year}' groups (find-then-create with no unique constraint)
findings.expected: Exactly one batch group per year; every alumnus of that batch lands in it (batch groups back batch-targeted posts and Catch-ups).
findings.actual: joinBatchGroup does `findFirst({ where: { name } })` then `create(...)` with no unique constraint behind it — the code's own comment concedes 'Group.name is not unique in the schema'. Two alumni of the same batch signing up concurrently (launch day, an invite email blast to a batch WhatsApp group) both read null and both create, yielding two groups named 'Batch of 1994' with membership split between them; later signups join whichever findFirst returns first. GroupMember's (groupId,userId) unique protects only membership, not the group row.
findings.evidence: actions.ts:215-230: `let group = await prisma.group.findFirst({ where: { name }, select: { id: true } }); if (!group) { group = await prisma.group.create({...}) }`. schema.prisma:193: `name String` — no @@unique. Contrast: the same file's user-create race was explicitly fixed with a P2002 handler (actions.ts:144-169, 'audit L9'), showing the pattern was known but not applied here.
findings.failure_scenario: Launch morning: three 1998-batch alumni sign up within the same second from a shared reunion link. Two 'Batch of 1998' groups exist; batch-targeted posts and the batch Catch-up reach only half the batch, permanently, until an admin manually merges rows.
findings.fixDirection: Add a partial/derived uniqueness: either a dedicated batchYear column on Group with a unique index (cleanest), or a unique index on name for the 'Batch of %' namespace via migrations-manual, then convert joinBatchGroup to create-catch-P2002-then-findFirst (mirroring the registerUser pattern).
findings.gateOrTest: Unit test firing two concurrent joinBatchGroup calls against a test row (or pin via the P2002-handling code path); the migration itself is the real gate.
findings.reproPlan: code-argument-only (provoking it needs concurrent real signups against the shared DB).

findings.title: Production images are served straight from throttled pub-*.r2.dev through plain tags — Cloudflare rate-limits that hostname and does not intend it for production traffic
findings.expected: At 2,000 users, feed/collection/avatar image traffic is served from a host built for production volume (R2 custom domain behind Cloudflare's CDN, or Vercel image optimization absorbing origin fetches).
findings.actual: Post images render as `` (post-card.tsx:367, eslint-disabled next/no-img-element) where publicUrl is the raw `R2_PUBLIC_BASE_URL` — a pub-*.r2.dev URL per AGENTS.md ('served from a pub-*.r2.dev URL; a custom domain can be added before launch'). Cloudflare's documentation states r2.dev public development URLs are rate-limited and not recommended for production. Every member's browser fetches every image directly from that throttled host; nothing tracks the custom-domain switch as a launch blocker (bugs.md has no r2/custom-domain item — verified by grep).
findings.evidence: post-card.tsx:366-378: `{/* eslint-disable-next-line @next/next/no-img-element */} `. next.config.ts:167: 'Cloudflare R2 (pub-.r2.dev now; a custom domain can be added later)' — the remotePatterns entry shows next/image is configured for it, but the feed path bypasses next/image entirely. Suspected (not confirmed) because the actual throttle threshold is Cloudflare-side and undocumented numerically; the launch-scale risk is the claim.
findings.failure_scenario: Launch week: a few hundred members scroll the feed and collection; aggregate image requests to the single pub-*.r2.dev hostname cross Cloudflare's development-URL throttle; images across the site intermittently 429 and render broken, worst exactly when the most people are looking.
findings.fixDirection: Owner action before launch: attach a custom domain (e.g. media.rishivalley.space) to the rv-alumni-media bucket in the Cloudflare dashboard and set R2_PUBLIC_BASE_URL to it (storage.ts already builds every URL from that one env var; existing DB rows carry the old host, so add the legacy pub-*.r2.dev host to keyForUrl/delImage handling or migrate stored URLs).
findings.gateOrTest: A check in npm run check or a boot log warning when R2_PUBLIC_BASE_URL ends in .r2.dev in production; visual suite covers the render either way.
findings.reproPlan: Read-only: curl -I one stored image URL to confirm the serving host is pub-*.r2.dev.

findings.title: sendMail has no timeout, and verificationMailState performs an inline Resend send during layout render — a hung Resend connection stalls every page load for unconfirmed members
findings.expected: Page render never blocks on a third-party mail API; a wedged Resend connection times out in a bounded few seconds (the Turnstile client sets AbortSignal.timeout(5000) for exactly this reason — turnstile.ts:98).
findings.actual: `api.emails.send(...)` (email.ts:181-187) passes no timeout/AbortSignal, and the Resend SDK's fetch has no default timeout — a black-holed connection hangs until OS TCP timeouts (minutes) or the platform function ceiling. verificationMailState, awaited inside the (main) layout's render-blocking Promise.all (layout.tsx:35-52), calls claimAndSend → sendMail synchronously when the member has a queued verify row and budget exists (email-queue.ts:597-599, by design: 'it repairs'). So during a Resend hang, every page view by an unconfirmed member blocks on that call; and because each such page view is also a claim, four page views burn the row's four attempts (interlocks with the retry-burn finding).
findings.evidence: email.ts:181: `const { data, error } = await api.emails.send({ from: FROM, to: opts.to, ... });` — no signal, no timeout, unlike the fetch in turnstile.ts:89-99. layout.tsx:35: `const [unreadCount, mailState] = await Promise.all([ ..., session.user.emailConfirmed ? Promise.resolve(null) : verificationMailState(session.user.id), ...])` — render-blocking. email-queue.ts:597-599: `if (row.status === "queued") { const outcome = await claimAndSend(row); ... }`.
findings.failure_scenario: Resend degrades to hanging connections for ten minutes on launch morning. Every fresh (unconfirmed) signup's first pageview after signup hangs 30-120s on the shimmer, then errors; four pageviews later their verify row is terminally failed.
findings.fixDirection: Add AbortSignal.timeout(~8000) to the Resend send (treat abort as a transient failure); in verificationMailState consider moving the repair send into after() and returning 'imminent' for the current render, or keep the inline send but rely on the new timeout to bound render latency.
findings.gateOrTest: Unit test asserting sendMail rejects/settles within the timeout when the transport never responds (inject a stalled fetch).

findings.title: R2/network failures during upload are blamed on the member's photo ('try a different one'), the misleading generic branch of describeProcessingError
findings.expected: An infrastructure failure (R2 500/429, S3 SDK network error) tells the member the service is briefly unavailable and to retry the same photo.
findings.actual: Every upload path funnels ALL thrown errors — including putImage/getImageBuffer S3 failures — through describeProcessingError, whose fallback is 'Could not process the photo. Please try a different one, or a JPG or PNG export of it.' During an R2 incident the member re-exports and re-picks photos that were never the problem.
findings.evidence: upload-shared.ts:96-108: only 'unsupported image format' and 'premature end|truncated|invalid' are special-cased; everything else → the photo-blaming fallback. finalize/route.ts:118-120 catches around a block containing `getImageBuffer(key)` and `putImage(...)` and returns `describeProcessingError(error)`; same shape at upload/route.ts:130-135 and collection/actions.ts:369-371.
findings.failure_scenario: R2 returns 500s for five minutes; a member trying to attach a photo to a post is told three different photos of theirs are unprocessable.
findings.fixDirection: In describeProcessingError (or at the call sites), detect S3/aws-sdk error shapes (err.name of S3ServiceException subclasses, $metadata.httpStatusCode, ECONNRESET/ETIMEDOUT) and return 'Our photo storage is briefly unavailable — please try again in a minute.'
findings.gateOrTest: Unit test feeding a mock S3ServiceException and asserting the storage-blame sentence.

findings.title: GitHub Actions disables scheduled workflows after 60 days of repository inactivity — the nightly retention sweep and 60-day account purge will silently stop once development quiets down
findings.expected: The retention sweep (and with it the GDPR account purge) keeps running unattended for the life of the site.
findings.actual: GitHub automatically disables cron-scheduled workflows in repositories with no commit activity for 60 days (documented GitHub behavior; an email warning is easy to miss). This project's deploys are git-push driven, so post-launch quiet periods are exactly the plan; after 60 quiet days the sweep stops, retention windows silently stop being enforced, and members' 60-day deletion requests are never purged — precisely the 'cron missed for N days' chaos case, but permanent. Suspected because it depends on future repo activity, not on code.
findings.evidence: retention.yml runs `on: schedule: - cron: '0 21 * * *'` from this repo; nothing monitors that it ran (the route writes a 'retention.sweep' audit entry, but nothing alerts on its ABSENCE — retention.ts:151-155 only records successes).
findings.failure_scenario: Six months post-launch, no commits for two months: purge-due accounts sit undeleted indefinitely; nobody notices because the failure mode is a job not running.
findings.fixDirection: Add a keepalive (the workflow can re-enable itself via a scheduled commit or use the GH API to keep-alive), or move the sweep to the app's existing lazy-tick pattern as a backstop (e.g. the admin dashboard checks the last 'retention.sweep' audit row's age and runs/flags it when stale), or surface 'last sweep ran N days ago' in /admin as a red state.
findings.gateOrTest: An /admin worklist item when the newest retention.sweep audit entry is older than 48h.
findings.reproPlan: Read-only: `gh api repos/:owner/:repo/actions/workflows` shows workflow state; currently active — the risk is future.
